questions.question: Explain why osmotic shock is effective mainly for Gram-negative bacteria?
questions.solution_html:
• This method is highly effective against Gram-negative bacteria due to their unique, 2 layered cell wall
  • (outer membrane and a thin peptidoglycan layer), which provides a specific location for target proteins and
  • a "weak spot" for the shock to act on. Sudden water influx, forces the outer membrane to rupture, releasing
  • periplasmic proteins and binding proteins.
questions.final_answer: periplasmic proteins and binding proteins

questions.question: Write down the principle and procedure associated with conventional filtration using filter paper.
questions.solution_html:
• paper.

  • paper acts as a semi-permeable porous barrier. The pores in the paper are specifically designed to be

questions.question: Explain the principle and application of micrometers in microscopy?
questions.solution_html:
• Principle of Micrometry ((3 marks)) - Ocular Micrometer: A glass disc with an arbitrary, unnumbered scale
  • (typically 100 divisions) placed inside the eyepiece. Stage Micrometer (Calibration Slide): A microscope
  • slide with a precisely etched, known scale (usually 1 mm divided into 100 parts, where each division equals
  • 0.01 mm or 10 µm). Calibration Principle: Because ocular divisions represent different real distances at
  • different magnifications, the ocular micrometer must be calibrated against the stage micrometer. The
  • relationship (ratio) between the two scales is used to calculate the actual size of the specimen.
  • Applications in Cell Measurement ((2 marks)) - Cell Size Determination, Organelle Measurement
  • Microorganism Identification

questions.question: Write a note on the refrigerated centrifuge.
questions.solution_html:
• It is an essential laboratory instrument that combines high-speed centrifugation with precise temperature
  • control (typically -20 to +40) to separate, sediment, or purify temperature-sensitive samples. It prevents
  • heat-induced degradation of samples (e.g., DNA, RNA, proteins, enzymes) during processing. Key
  • features include high RPM, rotor flexibility, and, for some, user-friendly interfaces.
questions.final_answer: features include high RPM, rotor flexibility, and, for some, user-friendly interfaces

questions.question: With diagram explain the principle and procedure of anion exchange chromatography.
questions.solution_html:
• With diagram explain the principle and procedure of anion exchange chromatography.
  • Principle: The resin (stationary phase) is coated with positively charged groups
  • (e.g., DEAE — diethylaminoethyl). Negatively charged molecules (anions) in a
  • sample are attracted to and bind to these positive groups. Neutral or positively
  • charged molecules pass through without binding. Bound anions are then
  • released by washing with an increasing salt (e.g., NaCl) gradient or change in
  • pH. Weakly bound anions elute first; strongly bound ones elute last.
  • Procedure
  • Equilibrate the column with a low-salt buffer (pH depends on Isoelectric point
  • of the molecule of interest). Load the sample onto the column.Wash with starting
  • buffer to remove unbound molecules. Apply a salt gradient (increasing NaCl
  • concentration)or pH gradient to elute bound anions stepwise. Collect fractions
  • at the outlet and detect using UV absorbance or other detectors. (2 +2 +1)
questions.final_answer: at the outlet and detect using UV absorbance or other detectors. (2 +2 +1)
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Explain the application of cell counting in hematology.
questions.solution_html:
• Cell Culture and Research Applications- Cell counting techniques are fundamental to cell culture, one of
  • the most important tools in modern biology and medicine. Accurate cell enumeration is essential for
  • maintaining healthy cultures, conducting reproducible experiments, and ensuring consistency in biomedical
  • research and biotechnology production.
  • Complete Blood Count (CBC): Counts RBCs, WBCs, and platelets in a blood sample. CBC includes red
  • blood cell count (RBC), white blood cell count (WBC), platelet count, hemoglobin concentration, and
  • various calculated indices. Deviations from normal ranges indicate various pathological conditions.
  • Anemia (low RBC or hemoglobin) may result from blood loss, nutritional deficiency, or bone marrow
  • disorders. Leukocytosis (elevated WBC) suggests infection, inflammation, or leukaemia.
questions.final_answer: disorders. Leukocytosis (elevated WBC) suggests infection, inflammation, or leukaemia
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: What is differential and density gradient centrifugation?
questions.solution_html:
• Differential centrifugation separates particles based on size and sedimentation rate using stepwise increases
  • in speed, while density gradient centrifugation separates particles by density as they settle through a
  • gradient medium. Differential Centrifugation: A homogenized sample is subjected to repeated
  • centrifugation at increasing speeds. Larger, denser particles (e.g., nuclei) pellet first at low speeds, while
  • smaller particles (e.g., ribosomes) remain in the supernatant and require higher speeds. Density Gradient
  • Centrifugation: The sample is placed on top of a pre-formed gradient (such as sucrose) or in self-forming
  • fgradient like caesium chloride. Particles migrate to positions where their density matches that of the
  • surrounding medium.
questions.final_answer: surrounding medium
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Explain the concept and applications of single cell analysis.
questions.solution_html:
• Single-cell analysis examines the genomic, transcriptomic, or proteomic profiles of individual cells
  • revealing cell-to-cell heterogeneity within populations that is masked by traditional bulk methods. It
  • identifies rare cell types, and maps cellular trajectories in development and disease ((1 marks))
  • Applications: ((4 marks))
  • Cancer research: Identifies rare drug-resistant tumor cells hidden within a tumor mass. Helps understand
  • tumor evolution and heterogeneity.
  • Developmental biology: Tracks gene expression changes as a single stem cell differentiates into specialized
  • cell types (e.g., blood cells, neurons).
  • Immunology: Profiles individual immune cells (T cells, B cells, NK cells) during infection or vaccination
  • to understand immune responses.
  • Neuroscience: Studies individual neuron types and their specific gene expression patterns in the brain.
  • Microbiology: Analyzes individual bacteria in a mixed community (microbiome) to identify species that
  • cannot be cultured.
  • Clinical diagnostics: Identifies circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in blood — a liquid biopsy for cancer
  • diagnosis.
questions.final_answer: diagnosis
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Discussion in detail the principle, instrumentation and working of HPLC. / Compare normal phase and reverse phase HPLC.
questions.solution_html:
• and reverse phase HPLC.
  • Principle ((2 marks))
  • HPLC is an advanced chromatographic technique that separates compounds based on their differential
  • partitioning between a liquid mobile phase and a solid stationary phase packed in a column.
  • The fundamental principle involves passing a liquid solvent containing the sample mixture through a
  • column filled with very fine particles under high pressure. Different components in the mixture interact
  • differently with the stationary phase based on their chemical properties such as polarity, size, or charge.
  • Components that interact weakly with the stationary phase move through the column faster and elute
  • earlier, while those with stronger interactions are retained longer and elute later. This difference in retention
  • times allows the mixture to be separated into individual components. The separation can occur through
  • various mechanisms including adsorption, partition, ion exchange, or size exclusion, depending on the type
  • of column and conditions used.
  • Instrumentation and Working ((4 marks))
  • The HPLC system consists of several key components that work together to achieve separation. A solvent
  • reservoir holds the mobile phase, which can be a single solvent or a mixture of solvents. The pump is a
  • critical component that delivers the mobile phase at high pressure (typically 1000-6000 psi) with precise
  • and constant flow rates. This high pressure is necessary to push the solvent through the tightly packed
  • column containing very fine particles. The sample is introduced into the system through an injector, which
  • allows precise volumes to be loaded onto the column without interrupting the solvent flow. The heart of
  • the system is the column, which is usually a stainless-steel tube packed with the stationary phase material.
  • As the mobile phase carries the sample through the column, different components separate based on their
  • retention times. After leaving the column, the separated components pass through a detector that identifies
  • and measures them. Common detectors include UV-visible detectors that measure light absorption
  • fluorescence detectors for fluorescent compounds, and refractive index detectors for compounds without
  • chromophores. The detector sends signals to a computer system that records and displays the data as a
  • chromatogram, showing peaks for each separated component. The chromatogram displays detector
  • response versus time, where each peak represents a different compound, the peak height or area indicates
  • the amount present, and the retention time helps identify the compound.
  • Comparison Table: Normal Phase vs. Reverse Phase HPLC ((4 marks))
  • Parameter Normal Phase HPLC Reverse Phase HPLC
  • Stationary Phase Polar (e.g., Silica) Non-polar (e.g., C18, C8)
  • Mobile Phase Non-polar (e.g., Hexane) Polar (e.g., Water, Methanol)
  • Compounds Retained Polar compounds Non-polar compounds
  • Elution Order Non-polar elutes first Polar elutes first
  • Sample Type Non-aqueous, polar samples Aqueous, non-polar samples
  • Sensitivity to Water High (water can damage column) Low (water is the mobile phase)
  • Column Equilibration Slower Faster
  • Usage Frequency Less common (~20-30%) Very common (~70-80%)
  • Applications Lipids, fat-soluble vitamins, isomers Drugs, amino acids, water-soluble
  • vitamins
questions.final_answer: vitamins
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Bring out the applications, advantages and limitations of 2 D Electrophoresis.
questions.solution_html:
• Applications ((6 marks))
  • Proteomics and Protein Expression Profiling (e.g.
  • diseased vs. healthy cells, treated vs. untreated samples) to identify upregulated or downregulated proteins)
  • Biomarker Discovery (to identify specific protein markers in serum, tissue, or bodily fluids for cancer
  • detection and other diseases), Post-Translational Modification (PTM) Analysis (protein modifications like
  • phosphorylation, glycosylation, methylation, and acetylation), Protein Interaction Studies (used to study
  • interactions by separating complexes and observing shifts in protein spots), Proteome Mapping and
  • Characterization: (map the entire proteome of organelles, bacteria, or cells, allowing for the cataloging of
  • protein responses to environmental changes) Food Safety and Adulteration (verify product purity in
  • pharmaceutical manufacturing, analyze batch-to-batch consistency, and detect food adulteration), and
  • Microbial Identification (based on unique proteins)
  • Advantages ((2 marks))
  • High Resolution, Quantitative Analysis, Low Cost, and Visual Map of Intact Proteins
  • Limitations ((2 marks))
  • Technical Complexity and Time, Poor Reproducibility, and Limited Detection of Specific Proteins
questions.final_answer: Technical Complexity and Time, Poor Reproducibility, and Limited Detection of Specific Proteins
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: With diagram explain the principle and procedure of anion exchange chromatography.
questions.solution_html:
• With diagram explain the principle and procedure of anion exchange chromatography.
  • Principle: The resin (stationary phase) is coated with positively charged groups
  • (e.g., DEAE — diethylaminoethyl). Negatively charged molecules (anions) in a
  • sample are attracted to and bind to these positive groups. Neutral or positively
  • charged molecules pass through without binding. Bound anions are then
  • released by washing with an increasing salt (e.g., NaCl) gradient or change in
  • pH. Weakly bound anions elute first; strongly bound ones elute last.
  • Procedure
  • Equilibrate the column with a low-salt buffer (pH depends on Isoelectric point
  • of the molecule of interest). Load the sample onto the column.Wash with starting
  • buffer to remove unbound molecules. Apply a salt gradient (increasing NaCl
  • concentration)or pH gradient to elute bound anions stepwise. Collect fractions
  • at the outlet and detect using UV absorbance or other detectors. (2 +2 +1)
questions.final_answer: at the outlet and detect using UV absorbance or other detectors. (2 +2 +1)

questions.question: Explain the application of cell counting in hematology.
questions.solution_html:
• Cell Culture and Research Applications- Cell counting techniques are fundamental to cell culture, one of
  • the most important tools in modern biology and medicine. Accurate cell enumeration is essential for
  • maintaining healthy cultures, conducting reproducible experiments, and ensuring consistency in biomedical
  • research and biotechnology production.
  • Complete Blood Count (CBC): Counts RBCs, WBCs, and platelets in a blood sample. CBC includes red
  • blood cell count (RBC), white blood cell count (WBC), platelet count, hemoglobin concentration, and
  • various calculated indices. Deviations from normal ranges indicate various pathological conditions.
  • Anemia (low RBC or hemoglobin) may result from blood loss, nutritional deficiency, or bone marrow
  • disorders. Leukocytosis (elevated WBC) suggests infection, inflammation, or leukaemia.

questions.question: What is differential and density gradient centrifugation?
questions.solution_html:
• Differential centrifugation separates particles based on size and sedimentation rate using stepwise increases
  • in speed, while density gradient centrifugation separates particles by density as they settle through a
  • gradient medium. Differential Centrifugation: A homogenized sample is subjected to repeated
  • centrifugation at increasing speeds. Larger, denser particles (e.g., nuclei) pellet first at low speeds, while
  • smaller particles (e.g., ribosomes) remain in the supernatant and require higher speeds. Density Gradient
  • Centrifugation: The sample is placed on top of a pre-formed gradient (such as sucrose) or in self-forming
  • fgradient like caesium chloride. Particles migrate to positions where their density matches that of the
  • surrounding medium.
questions.final_answer: surrounding medium

questions.question: Explain the concept and applications of single cell analysis.
questions.solution_html:
• Single-cell analysis examines the genomic, transcriptomic, or proteomic profiles of individual cells
  • revealing cell-to-cell heterogeneity within populations that is masked by traditional bulk methods. It
  • identifies rare cell types, and maps cellular trajectories in development and disease ((1 marks))
  • Applications: ((4 marks))
  • Cancer research: Identifies rare drug-resistant tumor cells hidden within a tumor mass. Helps understand
  • tumor evolution and heterogeneity.
  • Developmental biology: Tracks gene expression changes as a single stem cell differentiates into specialized
  • cell types (e.g., blood cells, neurons).
  • Immunology: Profiles individual immune cells (T cells, B cells, NK cells) during infection or vaccination
  • to understand immune responses.
  • Neuroscience: Studies individual neuron types and their specific gene expression patterns in the brain.
  • Microbiology: Analyzes individual bacteria in a mixed community (microbiome) to identify species that
  • cannot be cultured.
  • Clinical diagnostics: Identifies circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in blood — a liquid biopsy for cancer
  • diagnosis.
questions.final_answer: diagnosis

questions.question: Discussion in detail the principle, instrumentation and working of HPLC. / Compare normal phase and reverse phase HPLC.
questions.solution_html:
• and reverse phase HPLC.
  • Principle ((2 marks))
  • HPLC is an advanced chromatographic technique that separates compounds based on their differential
  • partitioning between a liquid mobile phase and a solid stationary phase packed in a column.
  • The fundamental principle involves passing a liquid solvent containing the sample mixture through a
  • column filled with very fine particles under high pressure. Different components in the mixture interact
  • differently with the stationary phase based on their chemical properties such as polarity, size, or charge.
  • Components that interact weakly with the stationary phase move through the column faster and elute
  • earlier, while those with stronger interactions are retained longer and elute later. This difference in retention
  • times allows the mixture to be separated into individual components. The separation can occur through
  • various mechanisms including adsorption, partition, ion exchange, or size exclusion, depending on the type
  • of column and conditions used.
  • Instrumentation and Working ((4 marks))
  • The HPLC system consists of several key components that work together to achieve separation. A solvent
  • reservoir holds the mobile phase, which can be a single solvent or a mixture of solvents. The pump is a
  • critical component that delivers the mobile phase at high pressure (typically 1000-6000 psi) with precise
  • and constant flow rates. This high pressure is necessary to push the solvent through the tightly packed
  • column containing very fine particles. The sample is introduced into the system through an injector, which
  • allows precise volumes to be loaded onto the column without interrupting the solvent flow. The heart of
  • the system is the column, which is usually a stainless-steel tube packed with the stationary phase material.
  • As the mobile phase carries the sample through the column, different components separate based on their
  • retention times. After leaving the column, the separated components pass through a detector that identifies
  • and measures them. Common detectors include UV-visible detectors that measure light absorption
  • fluorescence detectors for fluorescent compounds, and refractive index detectors for compounds without
  • chromophores. The detector sends signals to a computer system that records and displays the data as a
  • chromatogram, showing peaks for each separated component. The chromatogram displays detector
  • response versus time, where each peak represents a different compound, the peak height or area indicates
  • the amount present, and the retention time helps identify the compound.
  • Comparison Table: Normal Phase vs. Reverse Phase HPLC ((4 marks))
  • Parameter Normal Phase HPLC Reverse Phase HPLC
  • Stationary Phase Polar (e.g., Silica) Non-polar (e.g., C18, C8)
  • Mobile Phase Non-polar (e.g., Hexane) Polar (e.g., Water, Methanol)
  • Compounds Retained Polar compounds Non-polar compounds
  • Elution Order Non-polar elutes first Polar elutes first
  • Sample Type Non-aqueous, polar samples Aqueous, non-polar samples
  • Sensitivity to Water High (water can damage column) Low (water is the mobile phase)
  • Column Equilibration Slower Faster
  • Usage Frequency Less common (~20-30%) Very common (~70-80%)
  • Applications Lipids, fat-soluble vitamins, isomers Drugs, amino acids, water-soluble
  • vitamins
questions.final_answer: vitamins

questions.question: Bring out the applications, advantages and limitations of 2 D Electrophoresis.
questions.solution_html:
• Applications ((6 marks))
  • Proteomics and Protein Expression Profiling (e.g.
  • diseased vs. healthy cells, treated vs. untreated samples) to identify upregulated or downregulated proteins)
  • Biomarker Discovery (to identify specific protein markers in serum, tissue, or bodily fluids for cancer
  • detection and other diseases), Post-Translational Modification (PTM) Analysis (protein modifications like
  • phosphorylation, glycosylation, methylation, and acetylation), Protein Interaction Studies (used to study
  • interactions by separating complexes and observing shifts in protein spots), Proteome Mapping and
  • Characterization: (map the entire proteome of organelles, bacteria, or cells, allowing for the cataloging of
  • protein responses to environmental changes) Food Safety and Adulteration (verify product purity in
  • pharmaceutical manufacturing, analyze batch-to-batch consistency, and detect food adulteration), and
  • Microbial Identification (based on unique proteins)
  • Advantages ((2 marks))
  • High Resolution, Quantitative Analysis, Low Cost, and Visual Map of Intact Proteins
  • Limitations ((2 marks))
  • Technical Complexity and Time, Poor Reproducibility, and Limited Detection of Specific Proteins
